questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the activism and restraint labels are applied to a ruling
questions.stem: Translator's note 3 explains that a decision is criticised as activist when it is said to have substituted the judge's values for those of the legislature.

options.text: The criticism is misplaced, because any disagreement with an outcome makes a ruling activist.
options.misconception: equates disagreement with activism

options.text: The criticism concerns the source of the rule applied, not merely whether the outcome was popular.
The criticism is sound, because a court that reads a statute narrowly is always activist.
options.misconception: assumes narrow readings are always activist

options.text: The criticism is sound, because restraint requires a court to affirm any lower ruling.
options.misconception: makes restraint an automatic affirmance rule

questions.explanation: The activism and restraint debate concerns how a court exercises judgment in construing law, not whether people like the result. A careful construction can produce a surprising outcome without substituting personal preference.
questions.hint: Look at where the rule came from, not at the result.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what overruling a previous decision accomplishes
questions.stem: The translator asks for an explanation of what it means to overrule a previous decision.

answer.exemplar: To overrule is to declare that an earlier decision no longer controls, so that the rule it laid down is replaced by a different rule. The overruling court must identify the prior decision, explain why it is being departed from, and state the new rule that replaces it. The later decision governs cases that come after it.

questions.explanation: Overruling substitutes a new rule for an old one and requires the court to say why the earlier decision is no longer good law. It is not merely a criticism of the old decision.
questions.hint: An overrule replaces a rule, it does not just fault one.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the scope of a court's holding

stimulus.body: A translation note records that the decision holds only that a particular permit was issued without the procedure the statute required. The note stresses that the court did not decide whether the permit program as a whole is unlawful.

questions.stem: The note indicates that the court's holding in the quoted decision is what.

options.text: Limited to the procedure followed in that permit case, and not a ruling on the program as a whole.
Broad enough to condemn the permit program, because the defect would apply to every permit.
options.misconception: extends a narrow holding to the whole program

options.text: Limited to the parties, and expressly decides that the permit program is lawful.
options.misconception: adds a holding the note does not report

options.text: None at all, because the note describes a procedural defect without stating any conclusion.
options.misconception: claims the decision reached no conclusion

questions.explanation: The holding addresses the procedure followed in that one case and says nothing about the program generally. A court decides the case before it, and it does not announce broad rules for situations it has not examined.
questions.hint: A holding decides the controversy that was actually presented.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Law of the case on remand
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of the law of the case on remand

stimulus.body: An appellate court reversed a trial court judgment on the ground that the claims were time-barred. The case was remanded, and the trial court then dismissed the same claims on a different ground, holding instead that the claims had been stated with sufficient particularity.

questions.stem: The translator asks whether the trial court's second decision is permissible under the law of the case.

options.text: No, because the appellate court decided the claims were barred and the trial court must let that stand.
options.misconception: makes the law of the case cover all possible grounds

options.text: No, because a remanded case must always be retried before any further judgment is entered.
options.misconception: requires a trial on every remand

options.text: Yes, because the trial court may decide any question it likes once the case is returned.
options.misconception: gives the trial court unlimited freedom on remand

options.text: Yes, because the law of the case binds only the issues actually decided, so a new ground may be considered.

questions.explanation: On remand the trial court must follow the appellate court on the issues decided, but it may consider a different ground that was not decided. The law of the case bars revisiting settled issues, not new ones.
questions.hint: Decided issues bind; undecided issues remain open.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the requirement of a particularized injury for standing
questions.stem: A glossary entry asks two things about a plaintiff who complains only that the government broke a rule in general.

options.text: The plaintiff needs a concrete injury; and general complaints alone do not create standing.
The plaintiff needs a court willing to hear the complaint; and general complaints always suffice.
options.misconception: treats any complaint as sufficient for standing

options.text: The plaintiff needs a legislative fix; and general complaints must be raised by the agency.
options.misconception: redirects standing questions to the legislature

options.text: The plaintiff needs a written demand; and general complaints suffice once a demand is filed.
options.misconception: makes a written demand the source of standing

questions.explanation: Standing requires a concrete and particularized injury traceable to the challenged conduct, so a complaint about the government in general does not suffice. The question is never about a court's willingness or another forum's availability.
questions.hint: General grievance is not injury in a particular person.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Exhaustion when the agency fails to decide
questions.learningObjective: Explain how exhaustion works when an agency has not decided
questions.stem: The translator asks how exhaustion works when the agency never decided the question at all.

answer.exemplar: Where the agency has not made the decision the statute assigns to it, the claimant cannot be faulted for failing to seek review of a decision that does not exist. The claimant ordinarily must seek the agency's decision, and if the agency fails or refuses to act, the claimant may treat the failure as final and proceed to court. Where the statute compels a decision, the claim may proceed directly.

questions.explanation: Exhaustion requires that the agency first decide the matter, and if it refuses to do so the claimant may proceed on the refusal. Where the statute makes the decision mandatory, the claim may be brought without waiting.
questions.hint: There is no decision to appeal if the agency never decided.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of mootness on a pending appeal

stimulus.body: A note on an earlier volume explains that a case becomes moot when the controversy ends, and that the court then dismisses the appeal even though it once had jurisdiction, because a live controversy is required throughout.

questions.stem: According to the note, the effect of mootness on a case that was once properly before the court is what.

options.text: The court must decide the merits, because jurisdiction continues once it attaches.
options.misconception: makes jurisdiction permanent once it attaches

options.text: The court must order the respondent to pay the costs the decision would have imposed.
options.misconception: invents a costs remedy for moot cases

options.text: The court dismisses the appeal without reaching the merits, because a live controversy is required.
The court must vacate its own rulings and rehear the case when the controversy ends.
options.misconception: requires a rehearing once mootness appears

questions.explanation: Mootness ends the controversy, and the court then dismisses without deciding the merits because the requirement of a live controversy applies throughout the appeal. Jurisdiction does not freeze at the start of the case.
questions.hint: A live controversy is required at every stage.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the rules governing review of pre-trial detention

stimulus.body: A translator notes a case in which a person held without a conviction sought federal review of the detention, and the court explained that such review is narrow and generally requires that the person first seek relief in the state courts.

questions.stem: The translator asks what the note's case establishes about review of detention before conviction.

options.text: It establishes that pre-trial detention may be reviewed freely, because no conviction limits the claim.
options.misconception: assumes no conviction means no procedural limits

options.text: It establishes that such review is narrow and ordinarily requires prior relief in the state courts.
It establishes that pre-trial detention is unreviewable in any court, state or federal.
options.misconception: denies all review of pretrial detention

options.text: It establishes that the custody requirement does not apply until a sentence is imposed.
options.misconception: defers the custody requirement to sentencing

questions.explanation: Review of detention before conviction is narrow and generally requires the person to seek relief through the state courts first. Custody is what triggers the writ, and a lack of conviction does not free it from that requirement.
questions.hint: Narrow review, and the state process comes first.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the overrule described in a case note

stimulus.body: A translator notes that a reviewing court declined to read a federal statute to cover a practice its own predecessor had read to be covered, and the note comments that the court did so on the ground that the predecessor had wrongly extended the statute in the first place.

questions.stem: The translator asks how the review described in the scenario is best characterised.

options.text: As restraint, because declining to extend a statute never disturbs settled expectations.
options.misconception: assumes any non-extension is automatically restrained

options.text: As activism, because a reviewing court must always follow the reading of its own predecessor.
options.misconception: makes precedent unbreakable by the same court

options.text: As neither, because a court may not reconsider a decision of the court that issued it.
options.misconception: forbids a court to correct its own precedents

options.text: As an overruling of an earlier construction, which is a choice about which reading to adopt.

questions.explanation: Reconsidering an earlier construction is overruling, and choosing between competing readings is where the activist and restraint debate bites. Labelling the step restrained or activist skips the substantive question.
questions.hint: Rejecting your own reading is an overrule, whatever the label.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State what an overruling decision must do and what it leaves alone
questions.stem: The translator's note asks two questions about overruling: what the court does, and what happens to earlier cases.

options.text: The court replaces the earlier rule; and earlier cases decided under the old rule are not disturbed.
The court replaces the earlier rule; and every earlier case must be reopened and retried.
options.misconception: extends the overrule to all prior cases

options.text: The court merely notes the earlier decision was wrong; and the old rule still governs new cases.
options.misconception: makes a criticism rather than a change in law

options.text: The court defers the question entirely; and the earlier rule continues until the legislature acts.
options.misconception: defers overruling to the legislature

questions.explanation: Overruling replaces the earlier rule for cases that come after the decision, while cases already decided under the old rule ordinarily stand. Criticism of a decision without a stated replacement does not change the law.
questions.hint: New rule forward, earlier judgments undisturbed.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a holding should be characterised when cited later
questions.stem: A translator asks how a holding decided on one set of facts should be described when the case is cited later.

options.text: As a rule of general application, because the court stated its reasoning in general terms.
options.misconception: treats general reasoning as a general holding

options.text: As a holding on the issues and facts actually decided, not as a rule for all similar situations.
As binding on every future case, because a court decision binds everyone by default.
options.misconception: treats decisions as binding on the world

options.text: As persuasive only, because a case-specific holding can never bind even the parties.
options.misconception: denies binding effect on the parties

questions.explanation: A holding decides the issues and applies the reasoning to the facts before the court, so it is confined to those questions and that controversy. General language in the opinion does not convert it into a rule for all similar cases.
questions.hint: Holdings travel with the facts they were decided on.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Law of the case on remand
questions.learningObjective: Explain the doctrine of the law of the case in plain terms
questions.stem: The translator asks the reviewer to explain the law of the case on remand in plain terms.

answer.exemplar: On remand the trial court must follow the appellate court's rulings on the issues that were actually decided, and it may not reconsider those rulings or take a different view of them. The law of the case is a doctrine of consistency that binds the trial court on the remand, and the appellate court itself will generally treat the issue as settled in a later appeal.

questions.explanation: The doctrine binds the lower court to what the appellate court actually decided and stops the same question cycling endlessly between the two courts. It does not prevent the lower court from deciding matters the appellate court left open.
questions.hint: It is a consistency rule, not a gag order.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the standing requirement stated in a note

stimulus.body: A note in the translated edition states that a person must show that the harm they suffered is concrete and particular to them, and that a complaint that the law was broken in general, without more, does not entitle that person to sue.

questions.stem: The note's requirement corresponds to which of the following statements about standing.

options.text: Any member of the public may sue to enforce the law, because statutes are enforced by citizens.
options.misconception: makes enforcement a private right for all citizens

options.text: A plaintiff must show only that the conduct was unlawful, because unlawfulness creates standing.
options.misconception: treats unlawfulness alone as sufficient for standing

options.text: A plaintiff must show a concrete injury particular to that plaintiff, not merely a general breach of law.
A plaintiff must show that the government has admitted fault, because admissions establish standing.
options.misconception: makes an admission the basis of standing

questions.explanation: The general-grievance bar reflects the requirement that a plaintiff show a concrete and particularized injury. Proof of unlawful conduct in general, or of fault, does not establish standing to sue.
questions.hint: Particular injury, not general complaint.

questions.topic: Exhaustion when the agency fails to decide
questions.learningObjective: Apply the exhaustion rule where a statutory deadline has passed

stimulus.body: A translator notes a statute that directs an agency to decide an applicant's claim within ninety days. The applicant waited eleven months and filed suit without the agency having issued any decision on the merits.

questions.stem: The scenario turns on which proposition about exhaustion and agency inaction.

options.text: The claim fails, because exhaustion always requires waiting for a decision that must be sought again.
options.misconception: requires an endless sequence of requests

options.text: The claim fails, because an applicant must wait forever rather than sue on agency silence.
options.misconception: makes delay always fatal to a claim

options.text: The claim succeeds only if the applicant also obtained a final decision from the appellate body.
options.misconception: adds an appellate requirement to exhaustion

options.text: The claim may proceed, because the statute sets a deadline and the agency did not decide the claim.

questions.explanation: Where a statute gives the agency a deadline and the agency has not decided the claim, the applicant has done what the statute required and may proceed. Exhaustion aims at a decision, not at delay.
questions.hint: A missed statutory deadline means the decision will not come.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State when mootness arises and what the court then does
questions.stem: A footnote in the translation asks two questions: when a case becomes moot, and what the court then does.

options.text: Mootness arises when the court lacks jurisdiction; the court then decides the merits anyway.
options.misconception: reverses the effect of mootness

options.text: Mootness arises when the controversy ends; the court then dismisses without deciding the merits.
Mootness arises when a party loses interest; the court then vacates the judgment entered below.
options.misconception: makes vacatur the automatic response

options.text: Mootness arises only after a final judgment; the court then enforces that judgment as usual.
options.misconception: confines mootness to the post-judgment stage

questions.explanation: Mootness arises when the controversy between the parties comes to an end, and the court then dismisses the appeal without reaching the merits. A party's loss of interest ends the controversy just as a voluntary dismissal does.
questions.hint: No live controversy, no decision on the merits.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why review of pre-trial detention is narrower
questions.stem: The translator asks why the rules for pre-trial detention are stricter than those for challenges to a final conviction.

options.text: Because pre-trial detention is always unconstitutional, so no court may ever uphold it.
options.misconception: presumes pretrial detention is always unlawful

options.text: Because pre-trial defendants have more money for counsel and so less need for review.
options.misconception: reverses the reason for heightened protection

options.text: Because a defendant has not been convicted and the record for review is not yet complete.
Because pre-trial detention reviews are heard in state court, so the rules come from the states.
options.misconception: misplaces the source of the procedural rules

questions.explanation: Review of pre-trial detention is narrower because the defendant has not been convicted and the record is incomplete. The state's process comes first, and the custody requirement still applies before any sentence exists.
questions.hint: An unfinished record limits what can be reviewed.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the activism and restraint labels resist easy application
questions.stem: A translator asks the reviewer to explain why the labels activist and restrained are hard to apply to a decision.

answer.exemplar: Because the labels describe a disputed mode of exercising judicial judgment rather than a mechanical test. Courts must interpret ambiguous text, respect precedent, and sometimes accept an interpretation that produces an unusual result. Whether a court has substituted its own values for the legislature's is a question about the source of the rule applied, which requires reading the reasoning closely.

questions.explanation: The labels are not mechanical and not about outcomes, and they turn on whether the court respected the enacted law while construing it. That has to be assessed from the reasoning, not from the label attached to the outcome.
questions.hint: Assess the reasoning, not the result or the name.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the cases an overrule reaches

stimulus.body: A translator's note quotes an opinion that says a decision 'may be overruled by a later decision of the same court, in which case the later decision governs cases that come after it, while earlier judgments remain undisturbed.'

questions.stem: According to the quoted passage, the effect of an overrule reaches which cases.

options.text: Cases arising after the overruling decision, while earlier judgments are left undisturbed.
All cases decided before the overruling decision, which must be reopened to be consistent.
options.misconception: requires reopening every earlier judgment

options.text: Only the parties to the original case, since the overruling decision binds no one else.
options.misconception: confuses the overrule with the original holding

options.text: All pending cases everywhere, since an overrule reaches every court in the country at once.
options.misconception: assumes an overrule binds every court immediately

questions.explanation: An overrule changes the rule for cases that come after it, and earlier judgments remain undisturbed. It is not a command to reopen concluded litigation or to bind every court in the country.
questions.hint: Read the passage for what happens to earlier judgments.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe the scope of a decision decided on particular facts

stimulus.body: A translator notes a decision that declared a particular contract clause unenforceable against one lender because that lender had not given the notice the statute required, and expressly declined to address whether the clause was enforceable against other lenders.

questions.stem: The translator asks how the scope of that decision is best described.

options.text: As a rule that no clause of that kind may ever be enforced, because one failure proved the defect.
options.misconception: turns one instance into a general prohibition

options.text: As a rule binding all lenders, because lenders are similarly situated in every case.
options.misconception: assumes all lenders are similarly situated

options.text: As a holding that the clause is valid against lenders who did give notice, which was decided too.
options.misconception: invents a holding the note does not report

options.text: As a holding confined to the lender and the facts found, with no ruling about other lenders.

questions.explanation: The decision rests on findings about a particular lender's notice and a particular clause, so it decides that controversy. Declining to address other lenders means no ruling about them, not a rule either way.
questions.hint: An express reservation leaves other cases open.

questions.topic: Law of the case on remand
questions.learningObjective: State the obligations imposed by the law of the case on remand
questions.stem: A translator's table of cases asks two questions: what the trial court must do on remand, and what the appellate court will accept on a second appeal.

options.text: It must follow the rulings actually decided; and the appellate court generally treats those issues as settled.
It must start the case over; and the appellate court must review everything a second time.
options.misconception: requires a complete restart and full rereview

options.text: It may take any view it prefers; and the appellate court will accept the new reasoning if it is fair.
options.misconception: lets fairness replace the law of the case

options.text: It must follow the rulings actually decided; and the appellate court will revisit those rulings if it thinks fit.
options.misconception: makes the law of the case optional for the panel

questions.explanation: The trial court must follow the appellate court's rulings on the issues decided, and the appellate court generally will not revisit them in a later appeal. The doctrine exists to prevent the same issue from cycling endlessly between the courts.
questions.hint: Consistency runs in both directions between the panels.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a general objection to government spending does not confer standing
questions.stem: The translator asks why a taxpayer's objection to how public funds are spent does not by itself support a lawsuit.

options.text: Because taxpayers lack any interest in public finances, however the money is spent.
options.misconception: assumes taxpayers have no financial interest

options.text: Because a lawsuit requires that the government have done something wrong.
options.misconception: makes unlawfulness the test for standing

options.text: Because a general grievance about the government is insufficient without a particularized injury.
Because a taxpayer must first exhaust every available audit and complaint process.
options.misconception: invents an exhaustion rule for general grievances

questions.explanation: The general-grievance rule requires that the plaintiff show a particularized injury rather than a general objection to government spending. It does not deny that taxpayers have an interest, and it does not require prior administrative steps.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Exhaustion when the agency fails to decide
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of exhaustion when an agency will not decide
questions.stem: A translator asks why exhaustion cannot sensibly require a decision that an agency will never make.

answer.exemplar: Exhaustion exists so that the agency, which has responsibility and expertise for the matter, has the first chance to decide it. If the agency has refused or failed to act, there is no decision to appeal and no further benefit to be gained from insisting. The claimant may proceed on the refusal, though a statute that makes the decision mandatory can justify going to court directly.

questions.explanation: The purpose of exhaustion is to give the agency its first chance to decide, and it cannot demand a decision that will never be made. Where the statute makes a decision compulsory, going to court directly may be justified.
questions.hint: Exhaustion aims at a decision, not at obedience.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the situation in which a dispute is not moot

stimulus.body: A note in the translator's materials states that a dispute is not moot merely because the parties agree no further relief is needed, and that a case becomes moot when the controversy has ended for reasons of fact or law.

options.text: The parties have settled, because agreement removes the need for any further proceeding.
options.misconception: treats settlement alone as the test for mootness

options.text: The dispute continues to have live consequences for the parties, even though the immediate issue was resolved.
The agency has changed its position, because a change of policy always ends the controversy.
options.misconception: assumes a policy change always moots the case

options.text: The court has issued its judgment, because a judgment ends all controversy by definition.
options.misconception: makes the judgment itself the test for mootness

questions.explanation: Mootness turns on whether the controversy has ended, and a dispute whose consequences continue is not moot. Settlement, a policy change, and a judgment each have their own conditions and none is automatic.
questions.hint: Live consequences keep the controversy alive.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the sequencing of state and federal review of detention

options.text: Neither court may act, because a person held without a hearing has no remedy at all.

questions.hint: The federal court needs a record the state process builds.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the basis of the activist and restraint labels

options.text: It is activist when it reads a statute narrowly; it is restrained when it reads the statute broadly.
options.misconception: ties each label to one interpretive method

options.misconception: ties both labels to the outcome of the case

questions.learningObjective: State the effect of a court expressly departing from its own decision
questions.stem: The translator asks what follows when a court expressly departs from one of its own earlier decisions.

options.text: The earlier decision is overruled and the new rule applies to all pending cases, including those already decided.
options.misconception: extends the overrule to concluded cases

options.text: The two decisions coexist, and a later court may choose whichever it prefers.
options.misconception: treats the earlier decision as optional forever

options.text: The earlier decision no longer controls, and the new rule governs cases that come after the ruling.
Nothing changes, because a court is bound by every decision it has ever issued.
options.misconception: makes a court forever bound by its own past rulings

questions.explanation: An express departure replaces the earlier rule for subsequent cases, and cases already decided under the old rule are left alone. A court is not bound forever by its own past rulings.
questions.hint: Later rule for later cases, earlier judgments untouched.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why holdings are written as conclusions about the facts
questions.stem: The translator asks why careful opinions are usually written as holdings about the facts rather than as general rules.

answer.exemplar: Because a court decides the case that is before it, and the safest way to explain that decision is to tie the legal conclusion to the facts found. A general rule stated without regard to those facts risks deciding questions the court has not examined and invites difficulty in later cases where the facts differ.

questions.explanation: A holding tied to the facts is faithful to the case the court decided and avoids resolving questions not presented. General statements are more exposed when later cases present different facts.
questions.hint: Tie the conclusion to the facts that were found.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Law of the case on remand
questions.learningObjective: Determine what a lower court may do on remand after a reserved issue

stimulus.body: An editorial note explains that the appellate court decided one issue and expressly declined to decide another, and that on remand the lower court was directed to proceed consistently with the decision on the first issue only.

questions.stem: The note implies that the lower court on remand was free to do what.

options.text: Reconsider the issue the appellate court decided, because the note was only editorial.
options.misconception: treats an editorial note as authority to revisit

options.text: Proceed on the issue the appellate court left open, provided it did so consistently with the first.
Return the case to the appellate court immediately, because a remand always ends in another appeal.
options.misconception: assumes a remand always produces an appeal

options.text: Take any view it wished on both issues, because a remand resets the entire case.
options.misconception: makes a remand a reset of all issues

questions.explanation: The direction binds the lower court only on the issue decided, leaving the reserved issue for the lower court to address consistently with that decision. A remand is not a licence to reopen the decided issue.
questions.hint: One issue decided binds, one reserved stays open.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State what a challenger must show after a procedural defect

stimulus.body: A translator records a case in which a group of residents objected to a city ordinance they said was adopted through a defective procedure. The court noted that the residents had not alleged that the defective procedure harmed them in any particular way.

questions.stem: The translator asks what the court would most likely require the residents to show next.

options.text: That the city officials acted with bad faith in adopting the ordinance.
options.misconception: makes bad faith the measure of injury

options.text: That the ordinance has been enforced against at least one of the residents already.
options.misconception: requires prior enforcement as the only injury

options.text: That they suffered a particularized injury caused by the procedural defect they challenge.
Nothing further, because procedural defects alone always give rise to standing.
options.misconception: makes procedural defects automatic sources of standing

questions.explanation: A procedural defect alone does not confer standing; the challengers must show a particularized injury caused by that defect. Bad faith and prior enforcement are not the governing measures, and the defect alone does not supply injury.
questions.hint: Link the defect to this plaintiff's own harm.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Exhaustion when the agency fails to decide
questions.learningObjective: State the requirement for proceeding against an agency that has not decided
questions.stem: A translator's commentary asks two things about a claimant whose agency has said nothing: what the claimant must show, and what follows if the statute requires a decision.

options.text: The claimant must show nothing at all, and must wait for the agency to act at its own pace.
options.misconception: removes both the showing and the route to court

options.text: The claimant must show only a delay, and may then proceed without any further requirement.
options.misconception: treats delay alone as the whole requirement

options.text: The claimant must show a final decision, and must then seek further administrative review first.
options.misconception: adds a further-review requirement to exhaustion

options.text: The claimant must show the agency failed to decide, and may proceed where a decision was required.

questions.explanation: The claimant must show that the agency has failed to decide the matter, and if the statute requires a decision within a fixed time, that failure permits the claim to proceed. Delay alone, without agency inaction, is not enough.
questions.hint: Agency inaction plus a mandatory decision equals a route.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the court's obligation when a claim becomes moot
questions.stem: The translator asks what a court should do with a claim that became moot while the appeal was pending.

options.text: Decide the merits anyway, because the appeal was properly filed when it began.
options.misconception: freezes jurisdiction at the start of the appeal

options.text: Dismiss the appeal without reaching the merits, because a live controversy is required throughout.
Order the respondent to pay the costs incurred, because the claim was made in good faith.
options.misconception: makes costs the standard consequence of mootness

options.text: Vacate the judgment below and return the case for a fresh filing by the same party.
options.misconception: requires vacatur and refilling when mootness appears

questions.explanation: A live controversy must exist throughout the appeal, so a claim that becomes moot is dismissed without a ruling on the merits. Filing the appeal properly does not preserve the controversy to the end.
questions.hint: The live controversy must survive the whole appeal.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the special position of pre-trial detention in habeas practice
questions.stem: The translator asks the reviewer to explain the special position of pre-trial detention in habeas practice.

answer.exemplar: Pre-trial detention differs from conviction because the detainee has not been found guilty and the record of what happened is still being assembled. Review through the writ is therefore narrow, and the detainee is usually required to seek relief through the state courts, where the charges, evidence, and detention record are in place. The custody requirement applies from the moment of confinement.

questions.explanation: Because no conviction has been reached and the record is still being built, review is narrow and the state process usually comes first. Custody is required from the moment of confinement, not from sentencing.
questions.hint: An unconvicted person and an unfinished record.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify what is at stake in the activism and restraint debate

stimulus.body: An editorial introduction notes that courts differ on how far they should go in resolving statutory ambiguity, and that the disagreement is usually characterised as a debate between judicial activism and judicial restraint rather than as a disagreement about the text itself.

questions.stem: According to the introduction, what is at stake in the activism and restraint debate.

options.text: How much interpretive judgment a court should exercise when the statutory text is open to more than one reading.
Whether courts may exercise any judicial review of legislative acts at all.
options.misconception: reduces the debate to the existence of review

options.text: Which party should win the case, since the labels are applied after the outcome is known.
options.misconception: makes the labels a description of outcomes

options.text: How quickly a case must be decided, since delay favours the more activist party.
options.misconception: turns the debate into one about timing

questions.explanation: The debate concerns the extent of interpretive judgment a court should exercise on ambiguous text, which is why it turns on the reasoning rather than the outcome. It is not about whether review exists at all, nor about speed.
questions.hint: The stakes sit in the construction of ambiguous text.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the status of a construction abandoned by the same court

stimulus.body: A translator notes that a reviewing court followed its own precedent in the first appeal, then in a later appeal the same court abandoned that precedent, explaining that the earlier construction had rested on an assumption the court now rejected.

questions.stem: The translator asks what the note implies about the status of the earlier construction.

options.text: It remains binding because it was applied in a decided case, and only the legislature can undo it.
options.misconception: makes application in one case permanently binding

options.text: It was never binding at all, since the same court may reconsider any of its rulings freely.
options.misconception: makes overruling costless and routine

options.text: It binds only the parties to the first appeal, and no one else may rely on it.
options.misconception: confuses the holding with the overruled construction

options.text: It no longer controls cases decided after the overruling, though earlier judgments remain undisturbed.

questions.explanation: An overruled construction ceases to control subsequent cases, while judgments already entered under it stand. Prior application in one decided case does not make the rule permanently binding.
questions.hint: An overrule is a change of law, not an erasure.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a court's holding from its discussion of other situations
questions.stem: A translator's note asks two questions about a decision that discusses a situation without deciding it.

options.text: The discussion is not part of the holding; and the decision binds only the parties on the issues decided.
The discussion is part of the holding; and the decision binds every court in the country.
options.misconception: treats discussion as holding and makes it nationally binding

options.text: The discussion binds the parties; and the decision binds everyone else as persuasive authority.
options.misconception: grants binding effect to non-parties

options.text: The discussion is binding precedent; and the parties may disregard it at their own risk.
options.misconception: treats discussion as binding yet optional

questions.explanation: A court's holding is what it decided; discussion of a situation it did not decide is not part of the holding. The decision binds the parties on the issues decided and does not bind other courts as if it were a statute.
questions.hint: Separate what was decided from what was discussed.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Law of the case on remand
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of the law of the case doctrine
questions.stem: The translator asks why the law of the case doctrine exists at all.

options.text: To let the trial court revisit settled issues whenever the record turns out to be incomplete.
options.misconception: treats the doctrine as permission to revisit

options.text: To keep a case from cycling endlessly between the two courts over the same question.
To allow the appellate court to expand its own rulings when a later case suggests an error.
options.misconception: makes the appellate court a continuing body

options.text: To give the trial court the last word on any question of law it considers important.
options.misconception: gives the trial court the final word on law

questions.explanation: The doctrine exists for consistency and efficiency, so that a question once decided does not return to the same two courts in a loop. It constrains the trial court on remand rather than enlarging anyone's freedom.
questions.hint: Consistency and finality are the goals.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why courts require a concrete injury for standing
questions.stem: The translator asks the reviewer to explain why courts insist on a concrete injury in the standing analysis.

answer.exemplar: Because the standing requirement is what identifies the parties who may invoke the judiciary and limits the controversy it will resolve. If a general objection to lawful government sufficed, anyone could bring the same complaint on behalf of the public, and courts would be drawn into disputes they have no business adjudicating.

questions.explanation: Standing identifies who may invoke the judiciary and defines the controversy it will decide, which is why a general objection is not enough. Without it, anyone could litigate on behalf of the public at large.
questions.hint: Standing defines who may ask and what is decided.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Exhaustion when the agency fails to decide
questions.learningObjective: Apply the ordinary requirement of exhaustion

stimulus.body: A note explains that exhaustion of administrative remedies ordinarily requires that the agency have considered the complaint, and that where the agency has not acted on the complaint, the requirement may be satisfied by the claimant's having asked the agency to act and having received no decision.

questions.stem: According to the note, exhaustion is ordinarily satisfied when what has happened.

options.text: The claimant sought a decision from the agency and the agency failed or refused to make one.
The claimant obtained a written decision from the agency on the full merits of the complaint.
options.misconception: requires a written merits decision in every case

options.text: The claimant filed suit within a short time after sending the complaint to the agency.
options.misconception: substitutes a time limit for agency action

options.text: The claimant exhausted every possible appeal from the agency's initial refusal.
options.misconception: requires exhaustion of administrative appeals

questions.explanation: Exhaustion normally requires a request for a decision and the agency's failure or refusal to make one. A written merits decision is not always required, and the note does not demand further administrative appeals or a fixed time limit.
questions.hint: Ask for the decision, then show that none came.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the test for treating a case as moot

stimulus.body: A translator notes a case in which the party challenging a licence later obtained the licence through an alternative route, so the court no longer had any order to give that would change the party's position.

questions.stem: The translator asks how the case described in the scenario should be treated.

options.text: The court should decide the merits, because the licence was obtained by the wrong procedure.
options.misconception: keeps the case alive because of procedural wrong

options.text: The court should dismiss the appeal as moot, because no effective relief remains for the party.
The court should award damages for the delay in obtaining the licence through the alternative route.
options.misconception: invents a damages remedy for a moot claim

options.text: The court should vacate the licence, because the challenger obtained it by an improper route.
options.misconception: grants relief the claim does not support

questions.explanation: Mootness turns on whether effective relief remains, and here the position the challenger sought to change has already changed. Procedural error in how the licence was obtained does not keep the case alive.
questions.hint: Ask whether any order would still change the party's position.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State who may seek pre-trial habeas review and where it begins
questions.stem: A translator's footnote asks two questions about pre-trial detention review: who may bring it, and where it is brought first.

options.text: The detained person may bring it; and the state courts are the first forum for the claim.
The agency may bring it; and the federal court is the first forum for the claim.
options.misconception: makes an agency the petitioner and skips state courts

options.text: Any member of the public may bring it; and the forum is chosen by the party complaining.
options.misconception: removes custody and standing limits on the claim

options.text: Only a convicted person may bring it; and the claim lies in the sentencing court.
options.misconception: requires a conviction before detention may be challenged

questions.explanation: The detained person is the party who may bring the claim, and the state courts come first because the record of the detention is developed there. Public members and agencies have no such role, and no conviction is required.
questions.hint: The detainee asks, and the state court goes first.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the interpretive approach associated with restraint
questions.stem: A translator asks which change of approach in construing an ambiguous statute would most support the restraint side of the debate.

options.text: Reading the statute to cover a practice the legislature did not clearly address, on the view that courts should fill gaps.
options.misconception: treats gap-filling as the restrained course

options.text: Ignoring a plausible reading because a narrower construction is administratively convenient.
options.misconception: confuses convenience with restraint

options.text: Accepting the narrower reading the legislature most plausibly intended, without stretching the text to reach further.
Refusing to interpret the statute at all, and leaving the question to the agency.
options.misconception: equates abstention with restraint

questions.explanation: Restraint is generally associated with taking the text and the legislature's likely purpose as the limit of the court's role, rather than stretching the words to reach further. Abstention and administrative convenience are not the restrained course.
questions.hint: The restrained course stays inside the enacted words.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why overruling decisions are written at greater length
questions.stem: The translator asks the reviewer to explain why an overruling decision is often written at greater length than an ordinary one.

answer.exemplar: Because an overruling decision must do two things at once: apply the new rule to the case before it, and explain why the earlier decision is no longer good law, which means addressing the reasoning that supported it. That explanation is what makes the departure intelligible to later courts and to the parties who relied on the earlier rule.

questions.explanation: An overruling decision must both apply the new rule and justify displacing the old one, so it must engage the earlier reasoning. That explanation is what makes the change intelligible to later courts and to parties who relied on the old rule.
questions.hint: Two jobs: apply the new rule and justify the break.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an express reservation in an opinion

stimulus.body: An editor's note states that the opinion announces a rule for the situation presented and adds that the court 'expresses no view on how the question should be answered in other circumstances.'

questions.stem: The note tells the translator to expect what from the opinion's reach.

options.text: That the rule announced governs all similar situations, since the reasoning was general.
options.misconception: ignores the express reservation in the opinion

options.text: That the opinion decided the wider question after all, because it announced a rule.
options.misconception: reads the reservation as a decision on other cases

options.text: That the opinion is not binding on anyone, because it reserved part of the question.
options.misconception: makes a reservation dissolve the binding holding

options.text: That the rule governs the case presented, while the court left the other circumstances open.

questions.explanation: An express reservation confirms that the court's rule is confined to the situation presented and that the wider question was left open. Such reservations are common and do not weaken the binding effect of what was decided.
questions.hint: A reservation marks the boundary of the holding.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Law of the case on remand
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the law of the case operates on a second appeal

stimulus.body: A translator notes that on remand the lower court reached the same result as before but on the ground the appellate court had used, and the appellate court on the second appeal simply affirmed.

questions.stem: The translator asks what the note's sequence illustrates about the doctrine.

options.text: That the appellate court's ruling governed the remand and the lower court followed it, so nothing was relitigated.
That the lower court was free to depart, because the appellate court had not ordered any result.
options.misconception: suggests the doctrine leaves the lower court unrestrained

options.text: That the doctrine applies only to cases that end in a retrial rather than a judgment.
options.misconception: confines the doctrine to retrials

options.text: That the second appeal was required because the doctrine gives each court one reconsideration.
options.misconception: invents a single-reconsideration rule

questions.explanation: The sequence shows the doctrine working as intended: the appellate court's ruling governed the remand, the lower court followed it, and the second appeal did not reopen the issue. It is about consistency, not counting appeals.
questions.hint: The issue came back settled, and the panel left it that way.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the two elements of the standing inquiry
questions.stem: A translator's class list asks two questions about a plaintiff who has suffered a real harm from a rule applied generally.

options.text: Whether the harm is large enough, and whether the court has enough time to hear the case.
options.misconception: converts standing into a size and timing test

options.text: Whether the plaintiff has a lawyer, and whether the other side can afford to appeal.
options.misconception: makes resources the test for standing

options.text: Whether the rule is generally applicable, and whether other people have the same complaint.
options.misconception: turns the general grievance into a class claim

options.text: Whether the harm is particular to the plaintiff, and whether it is fairly traceable to the challenged conduct.

questions.explanation: The plaintiff must show an injury particular to the plaintiff and a causal connection to the conduct challenged. The size of the harm, the presence of a lawyer, the rule's general applicability, and similar complaints are not the test.
questions.hint: Particularity and traceability are the two elements.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Exhaustion when the agency fails to decide
questions.learningObjective: State when a claimant may proceed without an agency decision
questions.stem: The translator asks when a claimant may go to court on a matter the statute assigns to an agency for decision.

options.text: Only after the agency has decided the matter and the claimant has appealed to a reviewing board.
options.misconception: requires two exhausted steps in every case

options.text: When the agency has failed or refused to decide the matter and the statute permits the claim to proceed.
Whenever the claimant believes the agency is acting slowly, without any need to seek a decision.
options.misconception: lets a claim proceed on suspicion alone

options.text: Never, because courts may not hear claims that an agency has not yet decided.
options.misconception: makes agency inaction a permanent bar

questions.explanation: A claimant may proceed when the agency has failed or refused to decide and the statute allows it, since there is no agency decision to review. A belief that the agency is slow, without asking for a decision, does not suffice.
questions.hint: Agency inaction plus a statutory route is the combination.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish mootness from a claim that lacks merit
questions.stem: The translator asks the reviewer to explain what distinguishes mootness from a claim that simply lacks merit.

answer.exemplar: Mootness concerns the continuing existence of the controversy, not the strength of the parties' arguments. A case becomes moot when the dispute has ended, for example through settlement, the disappearance of the injury, or a change in the law that removes it. A claim that is weak on the merits is still justiciable and is dismissed on the merits instead.

questions.explanation: Mootness asks whether the controversy still exists, while a weak claim is still justiciable and fails on the merits. The two are answered by different questions and lead to different dispositions.
questions.hint: One asks if the dispute lives, the other if it wins.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the conditions for pre-trial habeas review

stimulus.body: A footnote explains that a person detained before trial may ask a federal court for the writ of habeas corpus, but that such review is narrow and generally requires that the person first have sought relief in the state courts where the detention is challenged.

questions.stem: The footnote supports which statement about pre-trial detention review.

options.text: The writ may be used by a detained person, but only after the state process has been tried and failed.
The writ may be used only after a conviction, because custody before trial is not custody.
options.misconception: requires a conviction before the writ applies

options.text: The writ is unavailable whenever the person is held on a valid warrant, however the detention began.
options.misconception: makes a warrant an absolute bar to the writ

options.text: The writ may be used at any time, because the state courts have no jurisdiction over detention.
options.misconception: denies state jurisdiction over detention

questions.explanation: The writ is available to a detained person, but review is narrow and normally follows an unsuccessful attempt in the state courts. A warrant does not bar the writ, and no conviction is required before the writ applies.
questions.hint: Detainee asks federally only after trying the state route.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Characterise a court's refusal to extend a statute

stimulus.body: A translator notes that a court refused to read a statute to cover a modern practice the legislature had not anticipated, reasoning that the legislature had deliberately left the question open and that the court should not step into that space.

questions.stem: The translator asks how the reasoning in the scenario is usually characterised.

options.text: As activism, because refusing to extend a statute deprives regulated parties of legal protection.
options.misconception: treats refusal to extend as an activist outcome

options.text: As activism, because the court resolved the ambiguity itself rather than leaving it to the agency.
options.misconception: counts any construction as activism

options.text: As restraint, because restraint requires leaving every question to the legislature.
options.misconception: makes restraint identical to non-decision

options.text: As restraint, because the court limited itself to the text and declined to fill a deliberate gap.

questions.explanation: The reasoning is generally described as restraint because the court confined itself to the enacted text and declined to fill what it saw as a deliberate gap. The absence of a protective reading does not make the decision activist.
questions.hint: Did the court stay inside the words the legislature used?

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the requirements of an overruling decision
questions.stem: A translator's footnote asks two things: what a court must do when it overrules, and how it must treat the earlier reasoning.

options.text: It must identify the decision being overruled and give a reason; and it must explain why the earlier reasoning no longer holds.
It must apply the new rule only; and it may simply state that the earlier decision is no longer good law.
options.misconception: allows overruling without any explanation

options.text: It must seek the legislature's agreement first; and it must wait for that agreement before proceeding.
options.misconception: makes overruling depend on legislative action

options.text: It must follow the earlier decision and note the doubt in a concurring opinion; and it must leave the law unchanged.
options.misconception: treats doubt as sufficient to depart from precedent

questions.explanation: An overruling decision identifies what it is displacing and why, and it explains that the earlier reasoning no longer holds. A bare statement that a decision is no longer good law, or a legislative waiting period, does not meet that standard.
questions.hint: Name it, and explain why it no longer holds.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the force of a general statement the court did not need to reach
questions.stem: The translator asks what happens to a general statement in an opinion that the court did not need to reach.

options.text: It binds every future court, because it appears in a published opinion of the court.
options.misconception: treats any published statement as binding

options.text: It is void, because an opinion may not contain anything beyond what it decided.
options.misconception: makes surplus statements void

options.text: It is binding on the parties to the case, because they are bound by the whole opinion.
options.misconception: binds parties to the whole opinion's statements

options.text: It is not part of the holding and carries no binding force beyond the issues actually decided.

questions.explanation: Only the holding binds, and a general statement the court did not need to reach is not part of it. Such language may carry persuasive weight, but it neither binds other courts nor enlarges the parties' obligations.
questions.hint: Binding force attaches to holdings only.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Law of the case on remand
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a later panel treats a point already settled
questions.stem: The translator asks how a later appellate panel should treat a point settled by an earlier panel in the same case.

answer.exemplar: It should treat the point as settled and not reopen it, because the earlier panel's ruling was necessary to the judgment and the case was remanded on that basis. The exception is where the earlier decision was clearly erroneous or the later panel has a compelling reason to depart, in which case the departure should be explained openly rather than made silently.

questions.explanation: A later panel normally treats an earlier panel's necessary ruling as settled and will not reopen it, which is the same consistency the doctrine enforces on the trial court. Any departure should be explained openly, not made silently.
questions.hint: Decided points stay decided unless the error is clear.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the elements of the standing inquiry described in a note

stimulus.body: A note states that the requirement of standing asks whether the person seeking the remedy has been harmed in a way the law recognises, and that the harm must be such that a court granting the remedy could redress it.

questions.stem: According to the note, standing requires which of the following.

options.text: That the harm be large, since a serious injury is the hallmark of a good claim.
options.misconception: makes seriousness the requirement

options.text: That the government have been at fault, since a remedy is owed only where fault exists.
options.misconception: makes fault the requirement

options.text: That the person's own recognised harm be capable of being redressed by the remedy sought.
That the harm be suffered by the public as a whole, since public injuries are the most serious.
options.misconception: reverses the particularity requirement

questions.explanation: Standing requires a recognised harm in the plaintiff that the remedy sought can redress, which is why a general public grievance does not suffice. Neither the size of the harm nor the government's fault is the requirement.
questions.hint: Recognised harm plus a remedy that could fix it.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Exhaustion when the agency fails to decide
questions.learningObjective: Apply exhaustion where an agency refuses to act

stimulus.body: A translator records a case in which a regulation required a permit holder to renew annually, the holder asked the agency in writing for a determination, and the agency replied that it had no authority to renew the permit for that year.

questions.stem: The scenario turns on what the claimant's step and the agency's reply together establish.

options.text: That the agency has effectively refused to act, so the claimant may proceed to seek judicial review.
That the claimant must return to the agency and ask a second time before seeking review.
options.misconception: requires a repeated request before review

options.text: That the claim is barred, because a decision was obtained and review must now be taken elsewhere.
options.misconception: treats a refusal as a final merits decision

options.text: That the permit question is moot, because no renewal was made for that year.
options.misconception: treats the agency's inaction as mootness

questions.explanation: A request for a determination plus the agency's refusal to act establishes the failure that lets a claimant proceed to judicial review. One request suffices, a refusal is not a final merits decision, and the matter is not moot.
questions.hint: Request plus refusal equals a route to court.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State when a controversy ends and what follows for the appeal
questions.stem: A translator's note asks two questions: what makes a controversy end, and what the court then does about the judgment below.

options.text: The controversy ends when the appeal is filed; and the court then vacates the judgment below automatically.
options.misconception: links filing to vacatur

options.text: The controversy ends when no effective relief remains; and the court then dismisses the appeal.
The controversy ends when the respondent files its brief; and the court then affirms the judgment below.
options.misconception: links briefing to affirmance

options.text: The controversy ends when the court announces its decision; and the court then remands for further proceedings.
options.misconception: makes the announcement the end of controversy

questions.explanation: A controversy ends when no effective relief remains for the party seeking it, and the court then dismisses the appeal without reaching the merits. Neither filing, briefing, nor announcing a decision ends the controversy by itself.
questions.hint: Look for the disappearance of effective relief.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why custody is central to pre-trial habeas practice
questions.stem: The translator asks why the custody requirement is central to pre-trial habeas practice.

options.text: Because only persons held without bail may ever use the writ, so custody alone is not enough.
options.misconception: narrows the writ to the bailed

options.text: Because the requirement is waived once the person has been charged, whatever the charge is.
options.misconception: treats an indictment as ending custody

options.text: Because the requirement is satisfied only by a sentence that has begun to run.
options.misconception: requires a sentence already running

options.text: Because the writ challenges the fact of restraint, so someone not restrained has nothing to challenge.

questions.explanation: The writ reaches the fact of restraint, so a person who is not detained has nothing to challenge and the requirement falls away. Charging a person does not end restraint, and the writ is not limited to those held without bail.
questions.hint: The target of the writ is restraint itself.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the activist label is treated as a criticism
questions.stem: The translator asks the reviewer to explain why calling a ruling activist is usually treated as a criticism rather than a compliment.

answer.exemplar: Because the label is used to suggest that a court has exceeded the proper limits of its role, either by reading language more broadly than the legislature intended or by resolving an ambiguity the legislature had deliberately left open. That is why the charge is serious: it implies that the court substituted its own judgment for the enacted law, and it is answered by showing how the ruling follows from the text.

questions.explanation: The label carries an accusation that the court went beyond its role by substituting its own judgment for the enacted law, so it is answered by showing that the ruling follows from the text and precedent.
questions.hint: The label accuses the court of going too far.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the consequence of an overrule for concluded cases

stimulus.body: An editorial note states that where a later decision of the same court departs from an earlier one, the later decision governs cases that come after it, while 'earlier judgments entered in the interim are not to be disturbed.'

questions.stem: The quoted words describe which of the following consequences of an overrule.

options.text: That all earlier judgments must be reopened so that the same rule applies to everyone.
options.misconception: requires reopening of concluded litigation

options.text: That concluded cases are left alone, while the new rule governs cases arising afterwards.
That the earlier decisions are treated as if they had never been decided at all.
options.misconception: erases the earlier decisions from the record

options.text: That the earlier decisions remain binding until every case in the country is relitigated.
options.misconception: makes the overrule await mass relitigation

questions.explanation: The quoted words preserve the distinction between the rule for future cases and the finality of judgments already entered. Earlier judgments are not disturbed, and the earlier decisions are not erased either.
questions.hint: Rule forward, finality backward.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a decision actually held where a statute was inapplicable

stimulus.body: A translator notes that a decision relied on a state statute that the parties had not argued about, and the court said the state statute was inapplicable because a federal statute governed the question instead.

questions.stem: The translator asks what the decision actually held, given the observation in the scenario.

options.text: That the state statute is unconstitutional, because the court analysed it at length.
options.misconception: treats discussion of a statute as a holding on it

options.text: That the state statute is valid in general, because the court found it inapplicable here.
options.misconception: infers a general validity ruling from inapplicability

options.text: That both statutes may be applied together, because the court mentioned each of them.
options.misconception: infers compatibility from joint discussion

options.text: That the federal statute governs the question and the state statute need not be reached.

questions.explanation: A holding decides the issue and applies the law to the facts, and here the court applied the federal statute and found the state statute inapplicable. Neither a ruling on the state statute's validity nor a compatibility holding follows.
questions.hint: Holding tracks the issue actually decided.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Law of the case on remand
questions.learningObjective: State the subject and reach of the law of the case
questions.stem: A translator's closing note asks two questions: what the law of the case binds, and who is bound by it.

options.text: It binds every issue in the case; and it binds every court in the country.
options.misconception: expands both the subject and the reach

options.text: It binds the issues actually decided; and it binds the public at large as well as the parties.
options.misconception: makes the doctrine bind the public

options.text: It binds the parties only; and it binds them on every question, decided or not.
options.misconception: expands the binding questions on the parties

options.text: It binds the issues actually decided; and it binds the trial court on remand rather than the public.

questions.explanation: The law of the case binds the lower court, on remand, on the questions the appellate court actually decided. It does not bind the public, and it does not extend to questions the appellate court left open.
questions.hint: It binds the lower court, and only on decided issues.
